source.title: Subspace-Aware Sparse Autoencoders for Effective Mechanistic Interpretability

page_placements.theme: Fixed-size fragmentation and duplication: one concept spread over several latents of one SAE

record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes SAE feature splitting with new geometric and optimization arguments, and evaluates related splitting and absorption measures rather than reproducing a dictionary-size sweep.
record.gate_note: The study reports results on SAE splitting, decoder-cluster redundancy, and feature absorption. Table 1 reconstruction and sparsity metrics, group-selectivity scores, and interpretability examples are not rows because they do not measure the claim versions. Figure-only activation profiles and the line-covering curve are not extracted where the text gives no specific values. The study does not compare a small and large dictionary on the same activations or trace a smaller feature's inputs into larger-dictionary features.
record.test_reason: The study gives a theoretical argument and synthetic results that splitting of multidimensional features comes from the single-direction, coordinate-wise ℓ1 SAE objective, and that a group-sparse objective (SASA) removes it. This bears on V6. It also measures first-letter absorption in GPT-2 and Mistral-7B SAEs, which bears on V4. It never varies dictionary size, so V1, V2, V3 and V5 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors go further: they claim the ℓ1 SAE objective provably prefers, not merely permits, fragmenting a multidimensional feature into exponentially many near-collinear atoms. They also claim SASA reduces splitting and absorption, improves interpretability, and matches standard SAEs on roughly half the token budget.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not reproduce the original SAE dictionary-size comparison. It analyzes standard single-vector, coordinate-wise ℓ1 SAEs and proposes SASA, which uses block decoder subspaces, Top-s group gating, and a nuclear-norm regularizer.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by SAE architecture and model: synthetic atom counts differ substantially across ReLU, TopK, BatchTopK, JumpReLU, and Gated SAEs; the reported absorption rates also differ between GPT-2 and Mistral-7B.

fits_no_version.finding: Open GPT-2 and Mistral-7B SAE decoders contain clusters of near-collinear vectors. Median cluster-size/PCA-dimension ratio is 2.18 for GPT-2 and 1.67 for Mistral.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fixed-size SAEs trained on LLMs allocate more decoder directions to clusters than the clusters' intrinsic dimension requires (decoder redundancy).

record.problems: The theory relies on an idealized single-feature slice and stated assumptions; empirical tests cover GPT-2 and Mistral-7B rather than a broad range of model families. The absorption benchmark is limited to eligible letters, and the reported splitting and absorption metrics have no uncertainty estimates. The study does not test dictionary-size scaling or cross-size feature correspondence.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted due to the 60-row limit. Table 1 reconstruction and sparsity metrics and selectivity/interpretability results were left out because they do not directly measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: All of it. There is no dictionary-size sweep and no mapping of smaller-dictionary features to larger-dictionary children.
All of it. Real-model SAEs are examined only for decoder-cluster redundancy at one size, not for the V1 splitting pattern.
All of it. There is no test of nested families mirroring a concept hierarchy. The SASA group geometry is about the authors' groups, not split SAE families.
Whether changing SAE size or sparsity fixes absorption. Neither was varied systematically.
Correlated or hierarchical inputs: only multidimensional manifold features are analysed. Matryoshka SAEs are not tested. There is no evidence on what real-model units are.

record.verdict_notes: Splitting here means tiling a continuous multidimensional feature, not the coarse-to-fine semantic splitting with dictionary growth in Bricken et al. That is why V1 and V2 links were removed. Section 7.3 compares one SASA group of 6 vectors with 35 standard-SAE atoms, but the 35 figure is cited from Engels et al. Figure 2c compares the empirical covering count with the bound, but gives no numbers in the text. Table 2 comparisons use external standard SAEs with double the tokens, and for Mistral a different ℓ0 (285 vs 80). Only Table 3 is a matched comparison.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures fragmentation across fixed-width dictionaries and gives theoretical splitting results, but does not sweep dictionary size or map a smaller-dictionary feature's inputs and direction to multiple larger-dictionary features.
Tests GPT-2 and Mistral-7B SAE results, but does not test open SAE releases as such or compare dictionary scaling across model sizes.
It describes geometry and category structure within SASA groups, but does not test whether split SAE features form nested, geometrically close families.
Measures absorption on the first-letter benchmark and compares standard SAE with SASA; it does not vary SAE dictionary size or sparsity to test whether those changes fix absorption.
No comparison of larger and smaller SAE latents as combinations, and no test of novel latents or canonical units.
The study analyzes the standard coordinate-wise ℓ1 objective and compares it with SASA; it does not test Matryoshka SAEs or establish what SAE latents represent as the model's own units.

rows.subject: standard SAE (theoretical)
rows.operation_detail: Derives a lower bound on the number of directions needed to cover a multidimensional feature slice using at most k co-activated directions.
rows.measure: k-sparse covering number Li(k)(ε)
rows.value: Li(k)(ε) ≥ C(t/ε)^((di−k)/k); when k ≥ di, an orthonormal basis gives Li(di)(0) = di
rows.note: A theoretical result under the stated local-richness assumption; it establishes a covering requirement, not a dictionary-size sweep or cross-dictionary feature matching.
rows.check: Theoretical covering bound, not a measurement. It argues single-direction decoders need many atoms for a multidimensional feature. It says nothing about dictionary growth, so it should not be linked to V1.

rows.subject: standard SAE (theoretical)
rows.operation_detail: Analyzes the decoder risk of the coordinate-wise ℓ1-regularized SAE objective and the path from a basis decoder toward an added direction.
rows.measure: Decoder risk relative to the true feature-basis decoder
rows.value: A continuous path reaches strictly lower risk; the paper states the objective drives the dictionary toward Θ((t/λ)^(di−1)) near-collinear atoms
rows.note: This is an objective-landscape result under the paper's theoretical setup, not an empirical measurement of trained model dictionaries.
rows.check: Theoretical result (Theorem 8): the ℓ1 objective rejects the true basis. This is an argument that the objective produces splitting, not an empirical rate. Remove the V1 link.

rows.subject: SASA (theoretical)
rows.operation_detail: Analyzes the global minimizer of the Top-1 block-gated SASA population objective on a single-feature slice.
rows.measure: Number of active blocks and recovered feature subspace
rows.value: Every global minimizer activates one block whose decoder recovers Vi
rows.note: A theoretical result for SASA, not an empirical size or sparsity intervention.
rows.check: Theory for the authors' own SASA objective. It bears on V6 only as an objective that removes splitting on a single-feature slice.

rows.measure: Number of decoder atoms used for the feature
rows.note: The figure description says vector-based SAEs distribute the feature over local slices; the count is not a comparison across dictionary sizes.
rows.check: Fixed width 256 on a synthetic manifold. There is no dictionary-size sweep, so the V1 link is wrong. Splitting here means tiling a continuous manifold, not coarse-to-fine semantic features.

relationships.condition: Theoretical single-feature slice and synthetic circle/sphere/helix manifolds (d=64, width 256)
relationships.reason: The ℓ1 objective provably prefers fragmented covers (R1, R2). All five vector-SAE variants spread one feature over 9–171 atoms (R4–R8, R10–R14, R16–R20), while the SASA group objective uses one group (R3, R9, R15, R21). Atom counts vary strongly by sparsity mechanism.
relationships.display_finding: The ℓ1 objective provably prefers fragmented covers, and all five vector-SAE variants spread one feature over 9–171 atoms, while the SASA group objective used a single group. Atom counts varied strongly with the sparsity mechanism.

relationships.condition: Standard vector SAEs on GPT-2 layer 7 and Mistral-7B layer 8, first-letter benchmark
relationships.reason: Standard SAEs show substantial absorption: mean 24.0–37.2% and full 23.3–49.6% (R24, R26, R28, R30), and 0.114–0.553 across five architectures (R32–R36). No size or sparsity sweep was run.
relationships.display_finding: Mean absorption was 24.0–37.2% and full absorption 23.3–49.6%, with scores of 0.114–0.553 across five architectures. No size or sparsity sweep was run.

relationships.display_finding: Changing the architecture cut absorption sharply in GPT-2 (0.046 vs 0.114 for TopK under matched training; 6.6% vs 37.2%) but less in Mistral (18.3% vs 24.0%), where ℓ0 and token budget were confounded.

relation.reason: Its theory, synthetic counts and first-letter absorption bear on V6 and V4.

tranche.reason: Theorems 4 and 8 and Figure 1 give a specific argument that splitting is produced by the single-direction ℓ1 SAE objective ('spurious multiplicity'), i.e. the challenge in V6. They also show that V6's 'correlated or hierarchical inputs' needs restating. This fits T5 better than T2.

source_check.notes: Table 2 standard SAEs are externally trained (Bloom et al.; Engels et al. for Mistral) on twice SASA's tokens. ℓ0 matches on GPT-2 (60) but not on Mistral (285 vs 80). Only Table 3 is matched training, and widths of the standard SAEs are never stated. Figure 1's sphere and helix rows are placed by the caption order, because the extracted layout is lost.

statements.correction: The text does not state widths for the standard SAEs (Table 2) or the Table 3 baselines. SASA width is m=12288 on GPT-2 and 32768 on Mistral (App. B.3). GPT-2 Table 2: SASA on 150M tokens vs an externally trained standard SAE on 300M; ℓ0 is 60 for both. Only Table 3 (0.046 vs TopK 0.114) uses matched data, tokens and schedule.
statements.problem: Numbers are right, but the conditions line says 'at fixed width', which this study never shows. The GPT-2 Table 2 gap also differs in tokens and SAE source.
The paper itself calls absorption closely linked to splitting, but R24 measures absorption only.

statements.correction: Table 2 standard SAEs: GPT-2 layer 7 has mean 37.2% and full 49.6% (ℓ0 60, 300M tokens). Mistral-7B layer 8 has mean 24.0% and full 23.3% (ℓ0 285, 1B tokens). Both are externally trained (Bloom et al. 2024; Engels et al. 2025), and their SAE type is not stated. The model difference is confounded with the SAE.
statements.problem: This is listed under 'same SAE type, different models', but the GPT-2 and Mistral standard SAEs are different external SAEs. Their ℓ0 and token budgets differ, and their architecture is not stated.

statements.correction: R1 (Theorem 4): with co-activation budget 1 ≤ k < di, covering a di-dimensional feature slice to error ε needs N ≥ C(t/ε)^((di−k)/k) directions; with k ≥ di, di directions suffice. R2 (Theorem 8): for 2 ≤ di < m and small λ/t, the orthonormal basis decoder is not a minimizer of the ℓ1 SAE decoder risk, and a continuous path reaches strictly lower risk. Setting: one multidimensional feature slice, with no hierarchy or correlation.
statements.problem: The statement cites this study's R1 and R2 but never names or describes them, so readers cannot see what the study contributes.

statements.correction: Table 2 absorption for the standard SAEs: GPT-2 mean 37.2% / full 49.6%; Mistral-7B 24.0% / 23.3% (R24, R26, R28, R30). The SAEs are different external ones (ℓ0 60 vs 285, 300M vs 1B tokens). No splitting measure is compared across the two models.
statements.problem: 'No row' is wrong: rows R24–R31 hold these values. They measure absorption, not splitting, and the model gap is confounded by the use of different SAEs.
